case.reference: Use only the supplied record through cycle 2, day 4. The daily urine-output sequence is 1.40 → 4.25 → 9.75 L/day; day 0 to day 4 changes by +8.35 L/day, or +596.4% when rounded to one decimal place. The two cycle-2 sodium measurements fall from 124.4 to 123.3 mEq/L; day-0 sodium is not supplied. Keep the previous cycle’s day-9 episode separate from this sequence. Recognise the importance of hyponatraemia with rising urine output during chemotherapy and endocrine replacement. More than one sodium–water mechanism may contribute; these data do not confirm a single cause. Spot urine sodium is a concentration, not a measured daily sodium loss. Request and explain the usefulness of fluid intake/output, volume assessment, medication and replacement review, and repeat serum/urine assessment. case.reference: Recognise severe symptomatic hypermagnesaemia in a patient with impaired consciousness, areflexia, mixed acid–base disturbance and ECG changes. Prioritise immediate airway/breathing and circulation assessment, monitoring and senior in-hospital escalation, with urgent renal/toxicology input for treatment and consideration of rapid magnesium removal. Initially normal creatinine does not make this presentation safe to observe routinely. Relevant exposure questions include medicines, laxatives/antacids/supplements and possible spa products or ingestions; the source and dose are not yet established. An unremarkable CT or negative common-drug screen does not resolve the metabolic emergency. Intravenous calcium and magnesium-removal strategies may be discussed as clinician-directed management, but do not require an exact dose, fixed fluid volume or dialysis prescription. A 52-year-old man has had watery diarrhoea three to four times daily for a year, with upper-abdominal discomfort and distal numbness. Previous gastrointestinal assessment identified bile reflux gastritis and a colonic lesion that was removed; histology showed a sessile serrated lesion with dysplasia. Diarrhoea persisted. Over the preceding six months he developed exertional breathlessness, fatigue and a 10 kg weight loss.

At the initial examination, blood pressure was 80/46 mmHg and heart rate 52 beats/min. Initial NT-proBNP was 887 pg/mL, high-sensitivity troponin T 23.9 ng/L, creatinine 1.3 mg/dL and eGFR 62.7 mL/min/1.73 m². No updated vital signs are supplied for the later investigation-review point.

Cardiac MRI showed diffuse wall thickening, high native myocardial T1, extracellular volume 49.85%–52.47%, and diffuse subendocardial late gadolinium enhancement involving the left ventricle and interatrial septum.

Serum/urine immunofixation and serum free-light-chain testing found no monoclonal gammopathy. Alpha-galactosidase A activity was 1.70 µmol/L/h (laboratory reference >2.0); GLA sequencing found no pathogenic variant. Plasma lyso-Gb3 was not measured. Technetium-PYP scintigraphy showed planar grade-1 myocardial uptake and a heart-to-contralateral-lung ratio >1.42; acquisition timing and additional technical details are not supplied here.

This exercise stops before the subsequent biopsy/subtyping investigations. No tissue diagnosis, further genetic result, later treatment or outcome is supplied.

case.title: Treatment timeline during circulatory support
case.task: Audience: an ICU clinical case review. Write 180–240 words in English using the headings Timing, Evidence and risks, and Missing record. Reconstruct the approximate UFH restart time and label recorded versus derived times. Calculate the 20:13-to-report delay and compare reporting with the estimated restart, preserving uncertainty about the actual restart. Assess whether this record establishes that the aPTT 58.9 s result informed restart. Explain what the platelet measurements do and do not show about the count at first alteplase initiation or a subsequent treatment effect. Identify the most useful missing records for assessing the decisions and bleeding risk. Do not prescribe a regimen, convert unverified infusion rates, invent an exact completion/restart time, or infer safety from an outcome not supplied.
case.opening:
A 28-year-old man presented with circulatory shock. At 08:21 on Day 0, BP was 70/45 mmHg and heart rate 142 beats/min. Right-heart abnormalities and a femoral venous thrombus were identified. VA-ECMO started at 10:20. CT pulmonary angiography at 11:58 showed main/branch pulmonary arterial filling defects. These are extracts for a retrospective ICU record review, not a live treatment instruction.

Day-0 record:
Time | Record
11:55 | Sample: platelets 21 × 10⁹/L, haemoglobin 150 g/L, fibrinogen 1.18 g/L and aPTT 43.5 s. Result-reporting times are not supplied for this sample.
14:50–15:10 | Two institutional therapeutic doses of apheresis platelets were transfused. Other haemostatic support was recorded over 13:15–17:00.
17:00 | Unfractionated heparin (UFH) was paused and the first alteplase infusion started. No post-transfusion platelet count immediately before this infusion is supplied.
17:20 | Arterial cannulation-site bleeding was treated with compression.
17:39 | Sample: platelets 62 × 10⁹/L, haemoglobin 136 g/L, fibrinogen 1.38 g/L and aPTT 47.5 s. Result-reporting times are not supplied for this sample.
18:10 | Vasoactive infusion rates were reduced, but ECMO and vasoactive support were still needed.
19:03 | A progress note records cessation of cannulation-site bleeding after compression; a second alteplase dose was ordered.
19:25 | The second infusion started. Each infusion stage lasted approximately one hour; exact completion timestamps are unavailable.
20:13 | A coagulation sample was obtained: fibrinogen 1.07 g/L and aPTT 58.9 s.
21:06 | The coagulation results from the 20:13 sample were reported.

The treating team later reported that UFH restarted after the second infusion, approximately one hour after its 19:25 start. No independent exact restart timestamp is available. A patient-specific anticoagulation target and the documented evidence used at restart are not supplied. The subsequent clinical course and later safety adjudication are not supplied.

facts.text: I used tirzepatide without medical supervision: weekly 2.5, 5 and 7.5 mg, each for four weeks, then intermittent 5 mg. Symptoms began about four weeks after my last dose.
Fasting glucose was 5.2 mmol/L two years earlier; a pretreatment fingerstick was 5.8. No recent pretreatment laboratory glucose, HbA1c or islet-function results were available.
My grandfather and several of his siblings had type 2 diabetes. No autoimmune family history was reported.
I used tirzepatide for weight reduction, not for a previously diagnosed diabetes condition. My height was 180 cm; weight was 94 kg before treatment and 75 kg at admission.
Admission vital signs were described as normal, without Kussmaul breathing.
Admission fasting glucose 13.99 mmol/L; HbA1c 10.8%.

Role/channel: record system; clinician-facing synthesis
Decision point: Researcher-defined review of records through 27 January 2023, before the March 2023 endocrine assessment and later treatment changes.
Opening: Records for a man treated for oesophageal cancer show a marked earlier TSH rise during thyroid replacement, followed by a suppressed TSH. Review the changing thyroid profile through 27 January 2023.

facts.text: In 2019, TT4 was 51 nmol/L with TSH 0.938 mIU/L; thyroid antibodies were elevated and ultrasound suggested Hashimoto’s thyroiditis. No intervention was undertaken. On 11 April 2022, before treatment and without replacement, TT3 was 0.93 nmol/L, TT4 53.87 nmol/L and TSH 0.82 mIU/L.

Pembrolizumab 200 mg with nab-paclitaxel 400 mg and carboplatin 400 mg every 21 days began on 15 April 2022. Radical oesophagectomy was performed on 7 July 2022, followed by adjuvant pembrolizumab, paclitaxel and carboplatin. The last chemotherapy cycle was completed on 23 September 2022; pembrolizumab continued.
On 6 May 2022, TT4 was 164.49 nmol/L and TSH <0.004 mIU/L. On 27 May, TT4 was 14.31 nmol/L and TSH 6.032 mIU/L; levothyroxine was started at 50 micrograms once daily.

The narrative reports good levothyroxine adherence, taken fasting and separately from other medicines. Table 1 identifies the dose at sampling: 100 micrograms daily on 22 August, 22 September and 27 October 2022, then 125 micrograms daily on 21 November 2022 and 27 January 2023.
On 22 August 2022, TT4 was <3.9 nmol/L and TSH 119.96 mIU/L. On 22 September, TT4 was 31.2 nmol/L and TSH 71.86 mIU/L. Both samples were recorded during 100-microgram daily levothyroxine treatment.
On 27 October 2022, TT4 was 68.0 nmol/L and TSH 2.36 mIU/L during 100-microgram daily replacement. Table 1 reference intervals are TT4 55.34–160.88 nmol/L and TSH 0.35–4.94 mIU/L.

On 21 November 2022, TT4 was 64.1 nmol/L and TSH 0.06 mIU/L. On 27 January 2023, TT4 was 45.8 nmol/L and TSH 0.08 mIU/L. Both samples were recorded during 125-microgram daily replacement. TT4 was within the reported interval in November and below it in January, while TSH was suppressed at both points.

requirements.requirement: Request paired current and earlier thyroid results with dates, rather than TSH alone.
requirements.presentation_based_rationale: The opening explicitly describes a changing profile; identifying the direction and meaning requires comparing TSH with thyroid hormone measurements.
requirements.acceptable_requests_or_alternatives: Current and serial TSH plus T4/free T4, or an equivalent dated thyroid-function review. A request for assay-verified free T4 counts even though quantitative free values are unavailable here.

requirements.requirement: Request levothyroxine dose/administration and cancer-treatment or surgical timing.
requirements.presentation_based_rationale: The task concerns results obtained during replacement and cancer treatment; exposure and dosing changes are needed to interpret the pattern.
requirements.acceptable_requests_or_alternatives: A medication review including replacement dose, adherence/administration and immunotherapy or relevant surgery chronology. No exact brand-name guess is required.

requirements.requirement: Seek assay clarification and further pituitary/adrenal evidence when the paired results raise concern for central dysfunction.
requirements.presentation_based_rationale: Discordant hormone and TSH behaviour leaves consequential alternatives unresolved; the review should identify how they could be distinguished.

case.reference: Use the dated TT4/TSH pairs and dose-at-sampling records. The earlier marked TSH rise and later low TT4 with suppressed TSH merit a qualified differential rather than automatic over-replacement or proof of isolated central hypothyroidism. Consider treatment/absorption, assay and illness context without claiming an unobserved cause. Pretreatment low total T4 with normal TSH prevents assuming completely normal baseline pituitary-thyroid function. The later diagnosis, normal adrenal tests and MRI cannot be required before disclosure. Quantitative interpretation or conversion of the suspect free-hormone fields is outside this adaptation; exact testing and treatment priorities await clinical confirmation.

case.adaptation: Published facts are paraphrased as record replies. The review cutoff, opening, task, release rules and candidate requirements are researcher-designed. March and later results are withheld by the chosen cutoff. No current symptoms, negative examination, baseline pituitary tests or treatment response are invented.

Role/channel: record system; clinician-facing synthesis
Decision point: Early hospital assessment of the symptomatic episode after documented telephone advice and a 20-mg oral hydrocortisone dose, before release of the episode’s endocrine test packet or subsequent response.
Opening: A woman receiving long-term treatment for Cushing’s disease has new nausea, abdominal pain, muscle pain, fatigue and low home blood pressure. Symptoms persisted after telephone advice, and she is now being assessed in hospital.

facts.text: The patient was 52 at the earlier diagnostic presentation, when ACTH-dependent Cushing’s syndrome and a pituitary origin were supported. Transsphenoidal surgery did not achieve biochemical remission; hypertension persisted and she declined immediate reoperation. The earlier work-up also diagnosed diabetes and insulin resistance. This age is not assigned to the current episode.

Ketoconazole was ultimately stopped because hepatotoxicity recurred. Metyrapone was later used for 36 weeks and stopped because its study ended, despite biochemical control and good adherence. Osilodrostat was then begun at 2 mg twice daily.

The symptoms began two years after osilodrostat initiation while she was receiving a stable total dose of 4 mg daily, without recent dose escalation. Earlier treatment had produced substantial biochemical and clinical improvement.

At symptom onset she reported nausea, abdominal pain, myalgia and fatigue. Home blood pressure was 98/67 mmHg, with heart rate over 100 beats per minute. No hospital vital-sign values are supplied in this source packet.

She was advised to stop osilodrostat, take hydrocortisone 20 mg orally and attend the next morning. She took the advised actions, but symptoms persisted and hospital assessment followed. The source does not specify the interval between hydrocortisone and the subsequent cortisol sample.
Dosing errors were excluded in the report; documented treatment adherence since the previous visit was 98%.

The episode’s Table 1B reports 08:00 cortisol 0.38 micrograms/dL (reference 4.82–19.5), ACTH 66.3 pg/mL (6.0–56.0) and DHEA-S 0.09 micromol/L (0.51–5.56). The narrative places confirmation during hospitalisation, without giving sample timing relative to the prior hydrocortisone dose.

requirements.requirement: Request the current cortisol-lowering regimen, recent dose changes/adherence and actions already taken.
requirements.presentation_based_rationale: New symptoms during endocrine treatment require the actual exposure and any rescue steroid history, including whether treatment preceded testing.
requirements.acceptable_requests_or_alternatives: Medication reconciliation covering the current cortisol-lowering drug/dose and any interruption or hydrocortisone already taken. Equivalent broad medication and treatment-timing requests count.
requirements.deadline: Before the final assessment, within the six question turns.

requirements.requirement: Request immediate clinical severity and contemporary cortisol/metabolic assessment, or request an equivalent urgent assessment.
requirements.presentation_based_rationale: Persistent gastrointestinal symptoms, fatigue and low blood pressure raise an immediate safety question irrespective of how long the dose has been stable.
requirements.acceptable_requests_or_alternatives: Current haemodynamic assessment plus cortisol and relevant glucose/electrolyte testing, or an appropriate urgent adrenal-risk assessment. Requesting unavailable observations counts; the request need not await a named diagnosis.
requirements.deadline: Before the final assessment, within the six question turns.

requirements.requirement: Review prior treatment control and endocrine history.
requirements.presentation_based_rationale: The task asks how the new episode relates to a long-stable course and previous disease; historical response informs that comparison without excluding a new adverse effect.
requirements.acceptable_requests_or_alternatives: Earlier cortisol/control records, prior endocrine treatment history or a clinically equivalent longitudinal review.
requirements.deadline: Before the final assessment, within the six question turns.

case.reference: A stable osilodrostat dose for two years does not exclude a new clinically important cortisol-lowering adverse effect. Integrate symptoms, home haemodynamics and the actual interruption/hydrocortisone sequence. Interpret the very low episode cortisol only once requested, while acknowledging unspecified sample timing after rescue steroid. Avoid assuming current normal glucose/electrolytes or copying the earlier age into this episode. Recognise the need for prompt clinical assessment without requiring a prediction of prolonged insufficiency or later relapse. Specific escalation and treatment recommendations await clinical confirmation; the source’s telephone regimen is historical evidence, not a compulsory management template.
case.hidden: Improvement after hydrocortisone adjustment to 25 mg daily, the four-year insufficiency course, later imaging, adrenal recovery testing at 50 months and later recurrence of hypercortisolism.
case.unavailable: Hospital haemodynamics, glucose and electrolyte results are not supplied. Adequate requests for those data or urgent clinical assessment still count; no normal results should be inferred.
case.adaptation: The urgent episode is represented through records rather than invented first-person speech. Published treatment timing is retained: the patient stopped osilodrostat and took oral hydrocortisone 20 mg before hospital confirmation. The contemporary endocrine packet is experimentally withheld until requested, although obtained during the published hospitalisation; no exact collection or reporting time is invented. Opening, task and requirements are researcher-designed. All subsequent response and long-term outcomes are withheld.

Role/channel: record system; clinician-facing synthesis
Decision point: Initial admission work-up, before next-day NGS evidence, definitive renal pathology and treatment response. Initial laboratory and non-contrast imaging records are requestable.
Opening: A 74-year-old woman is admitted with worsening dyspnoea, leg oedema and markedly reduced urine output after a febrile illness with gastrointestinal symptoms. Assess current danger and the main explanations for the renal presentation.

facts.text: Two weeks before admission she developed fever after a long-haul flight, peaking at 38.8°C, with nausea, diarrhoea and poor appetite. Fever and diarrhoea improved after acetaminophen and rifaximin. One week before admission she developed oliguria, reported as 350 mL/day, and dyspnoea, which progressed.

Admission findings were heart rate 106/min, temperature 36.5°C, blood pressure 130/56 mmHg, respiratory rate 28/min and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. There were bilateral pulmonary crackles, moderate lower-limb pitting oedema and dullness on bladder percussion. Abdominal, rebound and renal tenderness were absent.

She had hypertension and hyperlipidaemia for 10 years and type 2 diabetes for 20 years. Recorded medicines were felodipine, atorvastatin, aspirin, metformin and insulin. Acetaminophen and rifaximin were used during the preceding illness.

The initial laboratory table reports creatinine 689 micromol/L, urea nitrogen 66.3 mmol/L, potassium 7.11 mmol/L, phosphate 3.98 mmol/L, calcium 1.86 mmol/L and carbon dioxide combining power 5.5 mmol/L. The documented creatinine baseline was 65 micromol/L six months before admission. No measured blood-gas pH is supplied.

The table reports WBC 52.85 ×10^9/L, neutrophils 97.8%, CRP 96 mg/L and procalcitonin 5.9 ng/mL. Urine had marked pyuria and haematuria; flow-cytometry WBC was 41,905/microlitre, RBC 15,125/microlitre and bacteria 7,698/microlitre. UPCR was 1,655 mg/g creatinine and UACR 415.3 mg/g creatinine; reported 24-hour total protein was 598 mg.

Non-contrast CT showed bilateral renal enlargement and cortical thickening, with an ill-defined relatively hypoattenuating area at the left upper pole. Ultrasound showed bilateral enlargement and cortical swelling without hydronephrosis or abscess. Contrast CT was not performed because of AKI; acute-phase MRI was not performed because her clinical condition precluded safe transport/examination. These are missing investigations, not negative contrast/MRI findings.

The report states that a single 0.5-g IV meropenem dose was given on the day of admission before conventional blood and urine cultures were collected. NGS blood and urine samples were collected the day after admission. Microbiological results are outside this initial review packet; no culture-based susceptibility result is available in the report.

requirements.requirement: Request admission renal function, electrolytes/acid-base evidence and immediate clinical severity.
requirements.presentation_based_rationale: Oliguria with dyspnoea and oedema can involve urgent electrolyte, metabolic and volume-related hazards; the task explicitly asks about current danger.
requirements.acceptable_requests_or_alternatives: Renal function and potassium/acid-base testing with current observations or an equivalent urgent renal assessment pathway. An adequate absent ECG/blood-gas request counts.
requirements.deadline: Before the final assessment, within the six question turns.

requirements.requirement: Request urine/infection evidence and relevant recent medication or antimicrobial exposure.
requirements.presentation_based_rationale: A febrile gastrointestinal illness preceding severe oliguria leaves infection, volume loss and drug-related explanations unresolved.
requirements.acceptable_requests_or_alternatives: Urinalysis/protein or infection testing plus medication/antibiotic history; equivalent renal-infection assessment is accepted. No need to guess the later organism.
requirements.deadline: Before the final assessment, within the six question turns.

requirements.requirement: Request renal/urinary imaging or an equivalent obstruction assessment and establish what imaging was actually possible.
requirements.presentation_based_rationale: Marked oliguria and bladder percussion findings make a treatable obstructive contribution consequential; the task also asks for a defensible working explanation.
requirements.acceptable_requests_or_alternatives: Renal/urinary ultrasound, appropriate obstruction assessment, or relevant CT/imaging review with recognition that unavailable enhanced imaging is not negative.
requirements.deadline: Before the final assessment, within the six question turns.

case.reference: Received potassium 7.11 mmol/L, severe renal dysfunction and low carbon dioxide combining power require an urgent-risk representation; no measured arterial pH is supplied. Integrate recent illness, urine findings, diabetes, medication exposure and non-contrast imaging without collapsing multifactorial AKI into a confirmed focal bacterial or glomerular diagnosis. Ultrasound limits a major obstructive explanation but does not provide enhanced CT/MRI confirmation. Do not invent a positive culture or susceptibility profile, and preserve the antibiotic-before-culture chronology. Later biopsy and failed recovery are not initial evidence. Exact escalation pathway, differential priorities and treatment choices await clinical confirmation.
case.hidden: Next-day blood/urine NGS identification and conventional culture results; the authors’ sepsis/presumed-AFBN assessment; dialysis and antibiotic response, empirical steroid course, renal biopsy and one-year dialysis dependence.
case.unavailable: Initial ECG and measured blood-gas pH are not supplied. Pre-admission urinalysis records and serum IgA were unavailable. Appropriate requests count. Conventional culture and NGS results are withheld at this initial review point; contrast CT and acute MRI were not performed.
case.adaptation: The urgent admission uses records, not invented patient speech. Initial laboratory/imaging groups are experimentally requestable. NGS samples were actually collected the day after admission, so their results are withheld by the chosen cutoff; exact turnaround is not invented. A single admission meropenem dose before culture sampling is retained. Missing contrast CT/MRI and unavailable prior urine records remain missing. Subsequent interventions, pathology and outcomes are withheld; opening, task and requirements are researcher-designed.

facts.text: Symptoms progressed over about ten days, initially with diarrhoea and muscle pain; no previous kidney disease was known.
1 August 2025: creatinine 426.6 micromol/L, haemoglobin 80 g/L. 2 August: creatinine 456, haemoglobin 77. Admission was 9 August.

No measured pre-illness creatinine exists in the selected record. The plotted 92 micromol/L is the reference upper limit, not a patient measurement; 115 g/L is likewise a haemoglobin reference limit. A measured haemoglobin on 9 March 2025 was 123 g/L.
Ceftazidime and low-molecular-weight heparin were administered during the outpatient illness, after symptoms had begun.
At admission: blood pressure 167/90 mmHg, pulse 110/min and moderate oedema. DAT was C3-positive and IgG-negative in the initial work-up.
Admission urinalysis showed protein 500 mg/dL, dipstick haemoglobin 250/microlitre and 381 erythrocytes/microlitre. Urine volume was 650 mL/24 h.

Admission platelets were 213 x 10^9/L. LDH 352 U/L was reported with the admission evaluation; the later narrative labels this day 2, so an exact release time cannot be assigned. The selected early packet has no haptoglobin or peripheral-smear result.

case.opening: A 55-year-old man is admitted on 17 February 2019 after two years of abnormal urinalysis. Persistent proteinuria requires a diagnostic assessment; relevant renal and haematological records can be requested.

Opening: A 55-year-old man is admitted on 17 February 2019 after two years of abnormal urinalysis. Persistent proteinuria requires a diagnostic assessment; relevant renal and haematological records can be requested.

facts.text: Case 1 admission creatinine was 114 micromol/L and eGFR 61.6 mL/min/1.73 m². Twenty-four-hour urine protein was 1,259 mg and serum albumin 43 g/L. The report describes a two-year history of abnormal urinalysis but supplies no serial pretreatment creatinine trajectory.
Serum free kappa was 427.5 mg/L and free lambda 8.47 mg/L, with kappa/lambda ratio 50.47. Serum IgG was 15.80 g/L. These are Case 1 values.
Serum immunofixation showed a monoclonal IgG-kappa peak. Detailed marrow, skeletal and renal tissue findings are withheld in this adaptation, rather than being negative.

Urine glucose was ++ and urine pH 7.5. Urinary beta-2-microglobulin was 30.7 mg/L and alpha-1-microglobulin 110.9 mg/L. The source does not give a simultaneous serum glucose value for interpreting the glycosuria.
Serum calcium was 2.38 mmol/L, phosphate 1.36 mmol/L, potassium 3.7 mmol/L, bicarbonate 22.7 mmol/L and uric acid 300 micromol/L.
Haemoglobin was 131 g/L, platelets 191 ×10^9/L and LDH 143 U/L. These values belong to Case 1, not the second patient in the report.

Urinary amino-acid analysis was not performed. The authors did not establish a formal diagnosis of Fanconi syndrome. Case 1 urinary phosphate was 20.3 mmol per 24 hours, urinary potassium 39.2 mmol per 24 hours and urinary calcium 0.53 mmol per 24 hours; fractional excretion values are not supplied.

requirements.requirement: Request renal function and quantify/characterise the urine abnormality.
requirements.presentation_based_rationale: Persistent abnormal urinalysis and proteinuria require establishing renal severity and whether the pattern suggests glomerular or tubular involvement.
requirements.acceptable_requests_or_alternatives: Creatinine/eGFR plus protein quantification and urinalysis or appropriate tubular-protein assessment. Clinically equivalent urine/renal work-up counts; exhaustive tubular testing is not required.
requirements.deadline: Before the final assessment, within the six question turns.

requirements.requirement: Request monoclonal-protein testing or an equivalent haematological evaluation.
requirements.presentation_based_rationale: The task explicitly asks whether haematological evidence changes the renal differential; a defensible assessment needs the relevant protein evidence.
requirements.acceptable_requests_or_alternatives: Serum/urine electrophoresis with immunofixation and/or serum free light chains, or an appropriate paraprotein work-up. No need to name a hidden renal lesion.
requirements.deadline: Before the final assessment, within the six question turns.

requirements.requirement: Seek evidence of systemic clonal disease and a discriminating tissue/tubular assessment.
requirements.presentation_based_rationale: Monoclonal-protein findings do not by themselves identify the renal lesion or establish the full systemic disease category.
requirements.acceptable_requests_or_alternatives: Marrow or skeletal assessment, renal biopsy planning, simultaneous glucose or clinically equivalent proximal-tubular studies. Adequate requests count even when their results are withheld.
requirements.deadline: Before the final assessment, within the six question turns.

case.reference: Represent Case 1 as persistent proteinuria with modestly reduced filtration and strong kappa-restricted monoclonal evidence. Glycosuria and low-molecular-weight protein markers support investigating proximal tubular involvement but do not prove its cause or a complete Fanconi syndrome; simultaneous serum glucose and amino-acid testing are not supplied. A paraprotein-associated renal process is a working concern, while renal biopsy and systemic clonal assessment discriminate among possibilities. Do not import Case 2’s lambda excess, severe renal failure, cast findings or death. Do not require the hidden crystalline subtype, marrow percentage, bone lesions or staging. Exact essentiality and diagnostic recommendations await clinical confirmation.
case.hidden: Case 1 lytic skeletal lesions, marrow and cytogenetic staging, renal light/electron/immunoelectron microscopy, the final pathological subtype, treatment and outcomes. All Case 2 findings are excluded, not alternative facts for this patient.
case.unavailable: Detailed symptom/exposure history, simultaneous serum glucose and serial pretreatment renal measurements are not supplied. PET-CT, marrow/cytogenetic and renal-biopsy results are deliberately withheld, with exact result times unspecified. Appropriate requests still count.
case.adaptation: Only published Case 1 is used. Renal/urine, free-light-chain and immunofixation data are released as a researcher-defined pretreatment packet; the article does not supply exact collection/reporting times. PET-CT, marrow/cytogenetic and renal-biopsy results are experimentally withheld even though they are included in the source’s baseline work-up. Urinary tubular markers are provided without inventing their timing. No normal serum glucose, absent systemic features, full Fanconi syndrome or drug history is invented. Opening, task, release rules and requirements are researcher-designed.

Opening: An 80-year-old woman with lymphoma and cardiac comorbidity is admitted after witnessed syncope. She is hypotensive, has substantial leg oedema and has newly recognised proteinuria. Assess the immediate problem and the renal/systemic differential.

facts.text: The episode was preceded by progressive lightheadedness and tunnel vision, followed by brief loss of consciousness and rapid spontaneous recovery. Admission blood pressure was 86/58 mmHg. Examination showed significant bilateral lower-limb pitting oedema and generalised fatigue. No later/current repeat vital-sign values are supplied.

She had non-Hodgkin lymphoma previously treated with a rituximab-based regimen, heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, hypertension and coronary artery disease. The initial history does not establish a definitive lymphoma subclassification.

Initial neurological and cardiac evaluations, including investigation for arrhythmia and structural disease, were reported as unrevealing. Admission echocardiography showed EF 60–65%, normal left-ventricular thickness and trivial regurgitation. These findings are not a tissue evaluation for systemic deposition disease.
The admission column of Table 1 reports urine protein 3+, creatinine 1.8 mg/dL, BUN 45.0 mg/dL, albumin 3.0 g/dL and UPCR 10 g/g. No measured pre-illness creatinine is supplied.
Admission serum lambda free light chain was 131 mg/L, kappa 14.41 mg/L and kappa/lambda ratio 0.11. Serum immunofixation showed an IgM monoclonal lambda gammopathy.

Admission C3 was 78 mg/dL and C4 9.7 mg/dL; source reference intervals were not supplied. Hepatitis C antibody was positive, but HCV RNA and cryoglobulins were not detected. P-ANCA/C-ANCA were negative.

During the first admission she was also diagnosed with adrenal insufficiency and treated with hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone. The report supplies no confirmatory cortisol/ACTH results, doses or exact timing within the admission, and does not establish that this explained all findings.
The admission assessment was nephrotic syndrome of uncertain cause, and an outpatient renal biopsy was scheduled. Renal tissue and later marrow findings are not supplied at this decision point.

facts.text: She received a deceased-donor kidney transplant six years earlier for end-stage renal disease. The reported maintenance regimen before presentation was tacrolimus 1.5 mg twice daily, mycophenolate mofetil 360 mg twice daily and prednisone 8 mg daily.
About two weeks before this admission she developed throat discomfort and a productive cough. The symptoms did not improve with levofloxacin.

A tonic-clonic seizure occurred about one week before admission, followed by progressively agitated and abnormal behaviour. Neurological symptoms worsened despite symptomatic treatment at the local hospital, leading to transfer.
On Day 0 she was delirious and appeared pale. Temperature was 36.8 °C, pulse 91/min, respiratory rate 19/min and blood pressure 141/85 mmHg.

Opening: A 60-year-old man has one month of progressively blurred vision, dizziness and gait instability with frequent abnormal eye movements.

facts.text: Blurred vision, dizziness and walking difficulty have progressed over about a month. I have not had double vision, limb weakness or a febrile illness since this began.

The reported earlier medical history is unremarkable. There is no reported smoking, alcohol abuse or neurotoxin exposure, and no reported family history of autoimmune, neurological or neoplastic disease.

Admission vital signs and systemic examination were normal. There was continuous ocular flutter, a mild horizontal head/neck tremor, a broad-based gait and unsteadiness with eyes open or closed. Pupils and eye-movement range were normal; limb strength and pinprick/vibration sensation were preserved, reflexes were symmetric and Babinski signs absent.
Initial CSF opening pressure was normal, with white cells 12 × 10^6/L and normal protein, glucose and chloride. CSF pathogen mNGS was negative. Oligoclonal bands and the IgG index were not assessed.

High-resolution brain MRI with and without contrast showed no acute infarct, demyelination or structural brainstem/cerebellar lesion; the figure description also reports no abnormal contrast enhancement in those regions.

Routine peripheral blood tests, comprehensive metabolic panels and thyroid function were reported as unremarkable or normal. B lymphocytes were increased at 915/μL and 31.38% against the article's stated reference ranges; T-cell and NK-cell quantities were within those ranges.

The reported commercial fixed cell-based and immunoblot tests for established neural antibodies were negative, including the listed neuronal, demyelinating, onconeural and ganglioside targets. This statement concerns the standard specific-antibody panels; the tissue-based assay is outside this experimental packet.

At the initial presentation there were no reported weight-loss or gastrointestinal symptoms. Serum CEA, CA19-9 and AFP were within normal limits. Endoscopy and whole-body PET-CT were deferred; they were not negative investigations.

case.reference: Integrate the subacute ocular-motor and cerebellar findings into a provisional neurological syndrome. An unrevealing MRI and negative standard neural-antibody panels do not, by themselves, explain or exclude the clinically supported process. Mild CSF pleocytosis is supportive context rather than proof of a specific aetiology; negative pathogen testing and reported exposure/metabolic information should change the differential proportionately. Keep structural, infectious, immune-mediated, toxic/metabolic and other context-appropriate causes under consideration with defensible prioritisation. Normal tumour markers and deferred investigations do not establish comprehensive exclusion of malignancy. A specific tissue-assay result, final diagnostic label, future tumour or treatment response must not be demanded. Candidate requests and exact next investigations await clinical confirmation.

Opening: A 24-year-old woman is admitted for recurrent episodes of impaired consciousness preceded by headache and blurred vision. She has substantial cognitive difficulty, so obtain the longitudinal history from a caregiver and objective findings from records.

facts.text: The first recorded symptoms were brief headache and visual-disturbance episodes at about age six, lasting several minutes.
Learning difficulties appeared at about seven, with persistently poor primary-school performance. Between ages 15 and 21, no substantial neurological deterioration was reported.

At age 22 she had a probable focal seizure progressing to a bilateral tonic-clonic event while cycling, preceded by headache and blurred vision, with incontinence and foaming at the mouth. From 22 to 24, episodes recurred once or twice monthly.

The family noticed further memory and everyday cognitive difficulty in early adulthood, especially after recurrent seizures began. This is a reported change on top of longstanding learning difficulty; the report has no serial standardized cognitive assessments to quantify that change.

The parents were reported to be clinically healthy and were not consanguineous. Her younger brother reported mild memory difficulty but remained functionally independent; he had not undergone the genetic testing described in the report.
At admission, muscle strength, sensation and gait were normal, and the ophthalmological examination was unremarkable. MMSE was 12. Formal neuropsychological testing beyond MMSE was not completed.
The admission EEG showed sharp and slow waves in the bilateral occipital and parietal regions.

At age six, CT had shown small intracranial calcifications. At the adult admission, CT showed widespread basal-ganglia and cerebellar calcifications and two cystic lesions with fluid levels. MRI showed right thalamic and parietal cysts plus diffuse periventricular/deep-white-matter T2/FLAIR hyperintensity, without diffusion restriction or contrast enhancement.

requirements.acceptable_requests_or_alternatives: A collateral timeline covering early symptoms/learning, onset and recurrence of seizures, and reported adult functional change. Exact ages are not required in the question, and earlier records may substitute where caregiver recall is limited.

requirements.acceptable_requests_or_alternatives: Current neurological/cognitive examination plus EEG, or an equivalent specialist seizure-and-cognition assessment. No particular cognitive instrument or numerical score must be guessed.

requirements.acceptable_requests_or_alternatives: Current CT/MRI or a clinically equivalent structural-neurological investigation request, with comparison to earlier records where available. Asking for biopsy or a specific gene is not required.
requirements.deadline: Before the final assessment, within the six question turns.

case.reference: Preserve the distinction between childhood learning difficulty, a reported relatively stable adolescent interval, adult seizure onset and family-reported further cognitive deterioration. MMSE 12 establishes a low current score but does not quantify an acquired decline from childhood. Integrate received imaging and EEG with the clinical course to form a provisional structural, vascular, metabolic or inherited-neurological differential, with appropriate seizure assessment. Do not require the undisclosed biopsy, genetic result or final label. A healthy parental history does not settle inheritance, and the brother's symptoms do not establish the same condition. Requesting more detailed baseline/serial neuropsychological evidence is appropriate even though it is unavailable. Candidate essential requests and clinical prioritisation await confirmation.
case.hidden: Biopsy findings, compound heterozygous SNORD118 variants and their classifications, the final disease label, lacosamide initiation and response, discussion/declining of bevacizumab and three-month follow-up. No functional study of the novel variant was performed; a biological effect is not an experimentally established fact.
case.unavailable: Exact dates and order of investigations during the age-24 admission are not provided. Serial standardized cognitive scores and formal neuropsychological testing beyond MMSE are unavailable. A current pretreatment antiseizure-medication history is not supplied in this packet; no absence of earlier medication is inferred. Adequate requests for missing records still count.
case.adaptation: Published clinical facts and documented family observations are paraphrased into caregiver/record replies; no fluent first-person patient history is fabricated. The caregiver voice, pre-confirmation review, opening, six-turn task, requirements and release rules are researcher-designed. Requestable imaging and examination may already have been available to the real team; experimental withholding until requested does not change their chronology. No exact order or dates within the adult admission are invented. Biopsy/genetic confirmation and treatment outcomes are excluded. The report's caveat about unquantified adult cognitive progression is retained.

Opening: A 61-year-old woman develops sudden altered mental status, slurred speech and gait instability about one hour after retinal surgery, rapidly losing the ability to walk independently. Review the perioperative records for the emergency team.

facts.text: The recorded history included right cataract surgery in 2020 with good recovery. The report records no hypertension, diabetes, stroke, arrhythmia, thrombotic disease, smoking, alcohol use or hereditary disorder.

She was admitted on April 7, 2025 after seven days of right-eye visual loss and shadowing. Examination and ocular imaging showed a macula-involving rhegmatogenous retinal detachment; vitrectomy with laser and perfluorocarbon liquid was planned.

On April 8, standard three-port pars plana vitrectomy was performed under local anaesthesia with subretinal-fluid drainage. The retina reattached after heavy-liquid injection. Deterioration occurred while the team was preparing for silicone-oil tamponade.

She suddenly reported severe ocular pain, sweating and a near-death sensation during the operation. Pulse oximetry transiently fell to 88%. No post-deterioration full set of vital signs is supplied in this packet.

facts.text: The surgeon observed a dome-shaped choroidal elevation and suspected expulsive suprachoroidal haemorrhage. Estimated blood loss was 2 mL, confined to the posterior segment without anterior-chamber involvement or globe rupture. The record does not document direct observation of air entering the circulation.

facts.text: The procedure was immediately stopped, with 3 mL of perfluorocarbon liquid retained. The sclerotomies were closed, and intravenous hemocoagulase and tranexamic acid were given. Their doses are not supplied.

About one hour postoperatively she developed abrupt altered mental status, slurred speech and gait instability, quickly progressing to inability to ambulate independently. The packet stops at this emergency review, before the subsequent imaging and laboratory results.

Preserve the sequence of retinal surgery, intraoperative pain/hypoxaemia and suspected ocular haemorrhage, then neurological deterioration about one hour later. A vascular/embolic complication is a reasonable concern, but cerebral infarction, gas entry, a right-to-left shunt and a precise embolic route have not been demonstrated in the available packet. Keep other acute perioperative, metabolic and anaesthetic causes proportionately in the differential. Do not equate low recorded ocular blood loss with absence of a systemic emergency or prescribe the later reported antithrombotic regimen as a settled default before acute imaging and bleeding-risk assessment. Candidate requests, escalation pathway and management detail await clinical confirmation.

Opening: A 75-year-old man with late-onset focal seizures is admitted for worsening memory and seizures that have become daily. Review the available longitudinal records and the first comprehensive investigation packet.

facts.text: At age 60, a right-handed man with 16 years of education presented with transient forgetfulness. At 61, episodes involved olfactory hallucinations followed by blank staring and oral automatisms. Routine EEG initially showed no apparent epileptiform activity, but the clinical diagnosis was medial temporal lobe epilepsy.

Carbamazepine was stopped after a drug eruption. Valproate monotherapy, reported at up to 800 mg/day, was associated with seizure remission by age 64. Gabapentin was added at age 74 after recurrent seizures and right frontotemporal sharp waves on repeated EEG; its dose and the exact current valproate dose are not supplied here.

At age 70 he noticed mild memory difficulty: MMSE was 29 and WMS-R Logical Memory II delayed recall was 11/50. Forgetfulness worsened, and delayed recall was 6 at age 74. The narrative reports further worsening by admission at 75 but does not supply an exact age-75 cognitive score in this packet.
Focal impaired-awareness seizures recurred at age 72 after earlier remission, increased by 74 and became daily by the admission at 75 despite treatment.

At 74, brain MRI including susceptibility-weighted sequences showed mild diffuse atrophy without hippocampal sclerosis, microbleeds, amyloid-angiopathy features or significant vascular burden. FDG-PET showed no significant hypometabolism. At 75, repeat MRI and FDG-PET showed no significant interval change. No age-75 amyloid PET result is supplied.

At 75, 24-hour video EEG recorded six clinical seizures with ictal discharges arising in the left frontotemporal region and spreading through the left hemisphere. Table 1 also lists interictal spike/sharp-wave and sharp-transient counts, but explicitly states that sharp transients were not definitively epileptiform.

For the age-75 Ex. 1 sample, the published CSF results are Aβ40 13,671 pg/mL; Aβ42 1,549 pg/mL (reported reference >674); Aβ42/40 ratio 0.113 (reported reference >0.118); and p-tau 74.6 pg/mL (reported reference <50.0). These are the retrospective published sample results; real-time availability of the amyloid values at 75 is not asserted.

The first lumbar puncture was at 75, so pre-epilepsy CSF biomarker levels are unknown. The article states that stored Aβ samples were measured in duplicate in one analytical batch after one freeze-thaw cycle; p-tau was measured during routine practice at each puncture. Timing of cognitive testing relative to recent seizures was not systematically recorded.

case.reference: At the selected review, integrate recurrent focal seizures, worsening memory, documented delayed-recall decline and active age-75 video-EEG seizures with largely stable structural/FDG imaging. Opening: A liver-transplant recipient has recurrent vomiting of blood, dark-red rectal bleeding and right upper abdominal pain four months after transplantation. Bleeding and progressive anaemia have persisted.

facts.text: The patient is a 23-year-old man. Repeated bright-red haematemesis, about 50 mL per episode, was followed by dark-red haematochezia. Dull right upper quadrant pain, regurgitation, fatigue, dizziness, blurred vision and sweating accompanied the bleeding.

Orthotopic deceased-donor liver transplantation was performed in 2024 for end-stage alcohol-related cirrhosis. Before transplantation he had repeated decompensation and plasma exchange; oesophagogastric variceal bleeding was treated endoscopically in 2023.

The donor right hepatic artery arose from the superior mesenteric artery. Reconstruction joined donor common hepatic artery to recipient right hepatic artery and donor right hepatic artery to recipient gastroduodenal artery. The portal vein and common bile duct had end-to-end reconstruction.

Initial post-transplant immunosuppression comprised tacrolimus, enteric-coated mycophenolate sodium and corticosteroids, later adjusted. No antiplatelet or systemic anticoagulant treatment was documented in the immediate postoperative period; this does not establish the current medication list.

On postoperative days 6–8 he had fever and Enterococcus faecium bacteraemia, with positive SARS-CoV-2 testing. Fever resolved by day 9 after treatment. Imaging showed fluid collections without definite bile leakage or a localised infectious focus; bile culture was negative.

Earlier surveillance Doppler examinations showed patent hepatic arterial flow, with transient resistance or flow abnormalities that improved. No focal arterial lesion or pseudoaneurysm had been identified during that earlier surveillance.

Initial upper endoscopy found a duodenal bulb ulcer without observed active bleeding; no endoscopic haemostasis was performed. Continued bleeding prompted repeat endoscopy: removing a clot at the major duodenal papilla revealed fresh blood oozing from the papillary orifice.

Progressive anaemia during persistent bleeding is documented. A numerical blood pressure, pulse, coagulation panel and time-stamped haemoglobin specifically before the first angiogram are not supplied in this packet. Current severity measurements must be obtained rather than assumed normal.

requirements.presentation_based_rationale: Persistent overt bleeding with dizziness and progressive anaemia presents an immediate threat independently of its eventual cause.
requirements.acceptable_requests_or_alternatives: Current observations plus blood count/coagulation/crossmatch, or an explicit urgent haemorrhage-team assessment obtaining equivalent data. A request for unsupplied values receives credit; it need not produce a number.
requirements.deadline: Before the final assessment, within the six question turns. Emergency escalation must not be delayed to exhaust the question budget.

requirements.acceptable_requests_or_alternatives: Review initial/repeat endoscopy and seek transplant vascular/angiographic assessment when indicated; CTA/DSA or urgent specialist localisation are acceptable. Withheld definitive angiography does not turn an adequate request into failure.

case.reference:
This is recurrent overt gastrointestinal bleeding with progressive anaemia in a recent liver-transplant recipient. Dizziness, sweating and ongoing blood loss require immediate senior assessment, haemodynamic monitoring and preparation for haemorrhage management; the absence of supplied vital signs must not imply stability. Obtain current blood count, coagulation studies, crossmatch and relevant renal and graft tests while engaging gastroenterology and the transplant team.

The initial differential includes recurrent portal-hypertensive bleeding, peptic ulcer bleeding and a hepatobiliary or transplant vascular source. Prior varices create a plausible competing explanation, but neither history nor an ulcer alone localises the current bleeding. If the repeat endoscopic record is received, fresh blood from the major papilla strongly supports haemobilia and should prompt urgent vascular localisation with interventional radiology and transplant surgery. The exact lesion and arterial-biliary communication remain unconfirmed before angiography.

Review the reconstruction, immunosuppression and postoperative infectious history. Earlier patent Doppler flow does not exclude a subsequently developing vascular lesion. Past bacteraemia raises a question about infection without proving an infected pseudoaneurysm. Further diagnostic and haemostatic decisions must account for graft arterial perfusion. Do not use later embolization, surgical findings, pathology, deterioration or death to justify the initial conclusion. The later death mechanism was never definitively established; it is not a required diagnostic target.

Haemoglobin 64 g/L is tied to the first embolization in Table 1 and is not relabelled as an earlier pre-angiography value. No final lesion histopathology or aneurysm-wall culture was available, and the exact later cause of death remained unconfirmed.

Opening: A 70-year-old woman develops progressive jaundice over two weeks with intermittent abdominal pain, then three days of fever reaching 40.0 °C. She underwent liver surgery five months earlier.

facts.text: Yellowing of my skin and eyes increased over two weeks, with intermittent abdominal pain. Fever began three days before admission and reached 40.0 °C.

She had hepatitis C for 15 years. Left hepatectomy and cholecystectomy for a cirrhotic nodule were performed elsewhere five months before admission. Available records report no postoperative complications.

The original hepatectomy operative report is unavailable. The outside pathology report describes chronic hepatitis and nodular cirrhosis, with no definite neoplastic change. The available material cannot identify a specific operative vascular, thermal or biliary injury.
Admission total bilirubin was 234.0 μmol/L and direct bilirubin 182.4; ALP 155 U/L, GGT 172, AST 88 and ALT 64. Albumin was 38 g/L and INR 1.11.

Admission CRP was 188.60 mg/L, procalcitonin 9.49 ng/mL, white cells 4.10 × 10^9/L with 93.8% neutrophils, and platelets 76 × 10^9/L. Creatinine was 73 μmol/L and lactate 0.8 mmol/L. No further high fever was recorded after admission. Blood and bile cultures were not performed.

Available pre-ERCP MRCP shows intrahepatic and extrahepatic duct dilatation with sludge-like common-bile-duct material. The common bile duct measures about 19 mm and the largest intrahepatic duct about 9 mm. CT shows heterogeneous intraductal material.

The pre-ERCP contrast CT describes a patent hepatic artery supplying the remaining liver, without visible stenosis, occlusion or thrombosis. This is a large-vessel observation, not proof against every prior or localised ischaemic injury.

requirements.acceptable_requests_or_alternatives: Liver tests plus inflammatory markers and a current sepsis/organ-function assessment, or an equivalent urgent cholangitis assessment. Blood pressure not supplied must not be invented.

requirements.acceptable_requests_or_alternatives: Ultrasound or cross-sectional biliary imaging, MRCP/CT review, or an equivalent urgent specialist biliary investigation route. Exact anticipation of the eventual non-calculous material is unnecessary.

case.reference:
Jaundice, abdominal pain and recent high fever after hepatectomy require urgent assessment for biliary obstruction with possible acute cholangitis. Assess haemodynamics, mental state and organ function, obtain appropriate cultures if feasible, and involve the hepatobiliary or endoscopy service promptly. The absence of further high fever after admission does not erase the preceding illness. Treatment and drainage decisions should follow the current severity and local specialist pathway.

If the admission laboratory packet is received, marked predominantly direct hyperbilirubinaemia and raised inflammatory markers strengthen this concern. A near-normal total white-cell count does not negate the high neutrophil fraction or other inflammatory evidence. If imaging is received, substantial duct dilatation with heterogeneous common-duct material supports mechanical obstruction. Stones or sludge, postoperative narrowing, clot or tissue debris and tumour-related obstruction remain considerations; imaging alone cannot establish the material’s histology.

Review the outside operation and pathology. The operative report is explicitly unavailable, so a request for it is still appropriate and should be credited. Chronic hepatitis with cirrhosis and no definite neoplasia were reported in the outside specimen. A patent visible hepatic artery does not establish that all earlier microvascular injury is absent. The five-month sequence supports temporal association only; no specific surgical injury, necrotic epithelial pathology, cast morphology or later improvement should be asserted from the initial evidence.

Opening: A caregiver brings a seven-year-old girl with one week of dull upper abdominal pain and fullness after meals. She has poor appetite, looks pale, and has a palpable upper abdominal mass.

facts.text: She has had dull upper abdominal pain and fullness after meals for a week. Her appetite is poor. She has not had nausea or vomiting, and her bowel habits have remained normal.

We first noticed her eating hair when she was two. We interrupted the behaviour when we saw it and believed she had stopped completely in recent years. That is our belief, rather than a medically confirmed absence of the behaviour.
She has not had formal psychiatric intervention or follow-up to establish whether the hair-eating behaviour actually stopped.

Examination documents fatigue, pale lips and conjunctivae, asymmetric abdominal distension and a firm, non-tender, clearly demarcated epigastric mass about 12 × 6 cm, with limited mobility. No peritoneal irritation was noted.
Haemoglobin was 77 g/L, haematocrit 0.267 L/L, serum iron 3.1 μmol/L and ferritin 6.3 ng/mL. Faecal occult blood was weakly positive.
Total protein was 53.2 g/L, albumin 33.5 g/L and prealbumin 88.6 mg/L; the report describes hypoproteinaemia.

Available contrast abdominal CT shows a heterogeneous intragastric mass about 6 × 12 cm, considered suspicious for a foreign body or trichobezoar. No extension beyond the stomach was identified on this study. Endoscopic confirmation is outside this packet.

case.reference:
This child has an epigastric mass with early satiety, poor intake and pallor. Arrange prompt paediatric assessment, including examination for obstruction, peritoneal irritation and circulatory compromise, together with blood count and nutritional assessment. New persistent vomiting, severe or worsening pain, peritoneal findings or haemodynamic deterioration would require immediate escalation. The documented lack of vomiting or peritoneal irritation is useful but does not make a substantial mass harmless.

Ask the caregiver sensitively about hair and other non-food ingestion, when it was observed and what follow-up occurred. A reported past behaviour and the family’s belief that it stopped are different kinds of evidence. Neither proves current ingestion or verified cessation, and neither justifies blame or an unsupported psychiatric diagnosis.

If received, the laboratory findings establish substantial iron-deficiency anaemia, low protein measurements and weak occult faecal blood positivity. If CT is received, the lesion is intragastric and suspicious for a foreign body or trichobezoar, without detected extension on that study. These findings make an ingested-material mass plausible while specialist confirmation remains necessary. Coordinate paediatric gastroenterology, surgery and nutritional care, with appropriate behavioural support. The eventual endoscopic composition, treatment preference and outcome are hidden. A single successful prolonged procedure cannot establish the preferred or safest treatment for this child at first assessment.

The caregiver’s belief that the behaviour stopped is never upgraded to verified cessation.

I have worked with cattle for many years. I cannot recall whether I consumed unpasteurised dairy; livestock infection status was not documented.

Opening: An adult man treated for renal cancer presents to the emergency department with three days of fatigue, drowsiness and blurred vision, followed by one day of nausea and vomiting.

facts.text: The emergency presentation on 8 October 2024 followed three days of fatigue, drowsiness and blurred vision and one day of nausea and vomiting.

Right radical nephrectomy in January 2019 confirmed clear-cell renal carcinoma. Pembrolizumab 200 mg IV every three weeks plus axitinib 5 mg twice daily began in April 2023 for suspected pulmonary metastases. He had completed 22 immunotherapy cycles by the acute presentation.

Hypothyroidism was detected during earlier sunitinib treatment; levothyroxine maintenance was 100 μg/day. No family history of diabetes was reported. The discussion reports no previous diabetes and a normal fasting glucose about two weeks before admission, without providing the numerical prior value in this text.

At admission, vital signs were described as stable and he was afebrile. Examination recorded clear consciousness despite the preceding drowsiness, poor general condition and an acute appearance. Weight was 65 kg, height 180 cm and BMI 20.1 kg/m². No obvious cardiopulmonary or abdominal abnormality was found.
Admission glucose was 37.9 mmol/L, urine ketones 3+, pH 7.15, bicarbonate 9.8 mmol/L, base excess −17.6 mmol/L and lactate 4.6 mmol/L. Sodium was 128 mmol/L.

Admission HbA1c was 6.7% and fasting C-peptide was below 0.3 ng/mL. GAD, islet-cell and insulin autoantibodies were negative. These are reported admission findings, released on request experimentally without implying that all were available immediately.

The saved case paragraph does not supply admission potassium, renal function or a measured blood ketone concentration; it refers to supplementary laboratory tables. Those values are not supplied or assumed normal in this case packet.

requirements.presentation_based_rationale: Drowsiness, blurred vision and vomiting warrant immediate metabolic assessment even before the medication association is known.
requirements.acceptable_requests_or_alternatives: A coherent emergency metabolic/DKA assessment obtaining glucose, ketones, blood gas or bicarbonate and electrolytes/current observations. Requesting unavailable potassium or blood ketones counts; treatment must not be assumed safe from missing results.
requirements.deadline: Before the final assessment, within the six question turns. Emergency escalation must not be delayed to exhaust the question budget.

requirements.requirement: Request the cancer medication/treatment timeline and relevant previous glycaemic or endocrine history.
requirements.presentation_based_rationale: The task explicitly identifies active cancer treatment; medication effects and preceding glucose history affect interpretation without requiring a rare diagnosis guess.
requirements.acceptable_requests_or_alternatives: Medication reconciliation with immunotherapy/targeted-therapy timing plus prior diabetes/glucose or endocrine history. A general exposure/history request is sufficient; exact drug names and cycle count need not be anticipated.
requirements.deadline: Before the final assessment, within the six question turns. Emergency escalation must not be delayed to exhaust the question budget.

case.reference:
If the acute metabolic packet is received, marked hyperglycaemia, ketonuria and severe metabolic acidosis establish diabetic ketoacidosis requiring immediate monitored emergency treatment. Drowsiness and vomiting reinforce the risk; stable recorded vital signs or subsequently documented clear consciousness do not justify delay. Escalate to the appropriate senior emergency and diabetes or critical-care team, assess hydration and organ function, and begin protocol-based management with repeated metabolic monitoring.

Obtain potassium and renal function urgently. Their absence from this packet must not be treated as a normal result or ignored when planning insulin and fluids. Monitor electrolytes, glucose, ketones and acid-base recovery, while evaluating relevant precipitants. A complete dose prescription cannot be derived from the supplied excerpt.

Review pembrolizumab and axitinib exposure, the treatment timeline and endocrine history. If received, a relatively modest HbA1c alongside extreme glucose elevation, reported recent normal fasting glucose and very low C-peptide support abrupt insulin deficiency. Negative islet antibodies do not negate the acute metabolic findings. Checkpoint-inhibitor-associated diabetes is an important working explanation, but a particular fulminant subtype or proven cellular causal mechanism is unnecessary for urgent action. The cancer history, earlier treatment-associated hypothyroidism and suspected lung metastases should retain their reported context. Subsequent response, resumed oncology treatment and permanent insulin dependence must not be used as evidence available at this emergency assessment.
case.hidden: Fluid/insulin response, later ketone normalisation and treatment regimen, discharge, later pembrolizumab cycles and discontinuation, long-term insulin dependence and follow-up. Literature-review cases are not additional facts about this patient. No inferred numeric prior glucose, admission potassium or current age is invented.

Opening: A 65-year-old woman with COPD has one month of worsening breathlessness after cough and wheeze. She has not improved with outpatient treatment and now needs supplemental oxygen at admission.

facts.text: My breathing has worsened over about a month. It began with cough and wheeze; later I developed fever, chills and general weakness.
I smoke tobacco daily. I recently resumed vaping after having stopped seven years earlier.

No relevant occupational or environmental exposure, medication-related pulmonary risk factor, diabetes or other known cause of immunocompromise was reported. Details beyond those documented categories are not supplied.
The recorded background includes COPD and gastro-oesophageal reflux disease.
For presumed COPD exacerbation I received two courses of steroids; the second was combined with ten days of doxycycline. I did not improve clinically.

At admission she had hypoxaemic respiratory failure requiring 2 L/min oxygen by nasal cannula. Examination found diffuse basal crackles, minimal late expiratory wheeze and poor air movement. No numerical saturation or arterial blood gas is supplied in the saved presentation paragraph.

White-cell count was reported as 18,000 and procalcitonin negative. COVID-19 and influenza tests were negative. Early chest CT showed extensive bilateral ground-glass opacities. The later serological results and BAL are outside this early packet.

case.reference:
This is progressive respiratory illness with an oxygen requirement despite treatment for presumed COPD exacerbation. Hypoxaemic respiratory failure warrants active inpatient assessment, oxygen and repeated monitoring, with prompt respiratory or critical-care escalation if support needs increase. Establish current saturation, work of breathing, haemodynamics and blood gas where indicated; numerical values not supplied in the packet must not be invented.

Clarify smoking and the recent return to vaping, other inhalational or occupational exposures, medication risks and the timing of outpatient therapy. If received, failure to improve after two steroid courses and doxycycline, basal crackles and extensive bilateral ground-glass change argue for reassessing the initial label. Infection, inhalational injury, inflammatory or interstitial disease and other diffuse alveolar processes remain possibilities, alongside relevant cardiopulmonary alternatives. Negative viral tests or procalcitonin alone do not eliminate every infection.

Vaping exposure supplies a plausible clue but does not prove causation. The early CT pattern is not diagnostic of a specific proteinosis or injury mechanism. Target subsequent investigations to unresolved alternatives and clinical stability, including specialist consideration of lavage or serology where appropriate. At this decision point those tests have not returned. Do not import a later elevated antibody, inconclusive lavage, post-mortem result, response to treatment or death into the initial synthesis. Even the retrospective report leaves the relative contributors to acute lung injury unresolved.

case.reference:
This boy has a prolonged childhood-onset pain syndrome with functional limitation that merits reassessment beyond the earlier functional label. Clarify the distribution, severity and chronology of burning pain, heat or exertional triggers, sweating, gastrointestinal symptoms and school or exercise impact using caregiver history and age-appropriate engagement with the child. Obtain the neurological examination and a careful pedigree rather than treating one symptom as diagnostic.

If received, reduced pinprick and vibration sensation provide objective sensory evidence, while low sweating, abdominal symptoms and heat intolerance suggest an autonomic component. Maternal relatives with early renal disease and cardiomyopathy raise concern for an inherited multisystem disorder, including an appropriate lysosomal or metabolic differential. Other causes of peripheral or small-fibre neuropathy remain possible and should be evaluated proportionately. Consanguinity alone neither proves the disease nor defines its inheritance.

Arrange paediatric neurology or metabolic assessment, suitable laboratory evaluation and targeted biochemical/genetic testing when the combined findings justify it. Assess potential renal, cardiac and other organ involvement with appropriate specialist input; normal initial examinations do not substitute for the later formal screening programme. Conversely, family disease does not establish organ damage in this boy. The absence of observed skin or corneal signs does not settle the diagnosis. Do not assert enzyme deficiency, a particular mutation, affected relatives’ confirmed results or treatment response before those investigations are available.
case.hidden: Alpha-galactosidase A activity, lyso-GL-3, GLA sequencing and mutation; formal baseline renal, cardiac, brain, ophthalmological and audiological screening; enzyme-replacement treatment and response; subsequent confirmed familial variants and the maternal uncle’s laboratory values. Initial absence of those results does not establish presence or absence of organ involvement.

case.title: Generalised oedema during cancer treatment
case.decision_point: Investigation of oedema during treatment, before the suspected drug is withdrawn or any recovery is known.
case.opening: A woman in her early 70s with metastatic non-small-cell lung cancer developed generalised oedema during treatment.
case.initial_facts:
A woman in her early 70s with metastatic non-small-cell lung cancer developed generalised oedema during treatment.
Amivantamab started four months earlier. Oedema began after the first dose and extended to the abdominal wall over two weeks. Previous treatment included osimertinib and carboplatin/pemetrexed. She has hypertension treated with an ACE inhibitor.
Albumin fell from 4.6 to 2.1 g/dL. Creatinine is 1.83 mg/dL, previously 1.1. Blood pressure is 130/70 mm Hg, pulse 86/min, respiratory rate 18/min, temperature 36.8°C and oxygen saturation 97%. Lungs are clear and no jugular venous distension is reported.
Urine protein:creatinine ratio is 246 mg/g, with negligible microalbuminuria. Liver tests and echocardiographic function are normal. Faecal alpha-1-antitrypsin is negative and recent cancer imaging is stable. No subsequent drug-withdrawal response is supplied.

case.initial_facts:
A man in his 30s with type 1 diabetes received a kidney–pancreas transplant. Early delayed renal graft function required one dialysis session and then recovered.
He takes tacrolimus, mycophenolate and tapering prednisone, with antimicrobial prophylaxis. TMP-SMX 80/400 mg daily was stopped on post-transplant day 25 because of hyperkalaemia and replaced by pentamidine.

case.decision_point: Current admission for persistent diarrhoea and malnutrition, before withdrawal of olmesartan or subsequent recovery.
case.opening: A woman in her late 70s has had watery, non-bloody diarrhoea for 14 months, up to ten times daily and at night, with weight falling from 82.6 to 56.1 kg.
case.initial_facts:
A woman in her late 70s has had watery, non-bloody diarrhoea for 14 months, up to ten times daily and at night, with weight falling from 82.6 to 56.1 kg.
She has taken combination antihypertensives containing olmesartan for approximately three years. Hydrochlorothiazide was removed from the combination about 14 months ago; olmesartan continued. Duodenal biopsies showed villous blunting. Coeliac serology was negative while she was still eating gluten; later tests were also negative on a gluten-free diet.
Pancreatic enzymes for a low faecal elastase, rifaximin and dietary treatment did not resolve symptoms. Repeat elastase was normal. Symptoms improved during two admissions when her usual combination tablet was not supplied, then worsened after discharge. A short budesonide course overlapped with other treatment changes.
At this admission blood pressure is 104/62, pulse 88/min, albumin 2.3 g/dL, potassium 2.8 mmol/L, magnesium 0.7 mg/dL and phosphate 1.9 mg/dL. No response to deliberate medication withdrawal is yet known.

case.opening: A man in his 80s underwent hip-fracture surgery. He received unfractionated heparin before surgery and dalteparin afterwards. A later dalteparin dose was withheld because of haematuria after catheterisation. Levetiracetam was also newly prescribed.
case.initial_facts:
A man in his 80s underwent hip-fracture surgery. He received unfractionated heparin before surgery and dalteparin afterwards. A later dalteparin dose was withheld because of haematuria after catheterisation. Levetiracetam was also newly prescribed.
On postoperative day 6 platelets were 5×10^9/L and haemoglobin 98 g/L; the blood film showed schistocytes and a leucoerythroblastic picture. Anti-PF4 ELISA was strongly positive, with optical densities 2.64 and 2.71.
The first serotonin-release assay was reported as inconclusive, not negative: strong release occurred even without heparin and the initial inhibition experiment did not resolve interpretation.
By day 9 fibrinogen was 1.8 g/L, D-dimer 63,355 ng/mL, PT 14 s and INR 1.2. Proximal deep-vein thromboses were found in both legs. Subsequent specialised assays and treatment response are not supplied.

case.title: Severe gastrointestinal bleeding after neurosurgery
case.task_type: Emergency assessment with a negative bleeding scan
case.decision_point: Postoperative day 14, after shock, CT and limited endoscopy, before angiography.
case.opening: An adolescent boy received ketorolac in hospital after revision posterior-fossa surgery and was prescribed ibuprofen 400 mg as needed every six hours for about a week. No excess use is reported.
case.initial_facts:
An adolescent boy received ketorolac in hospital after revision posterior-fossa surgery and was prescribed ibuprofen 400 mg as needed every six hours for about a week. No excess use is reported.
On postoperative day 9 he had epigastric pain and constipation without haematemesis or melaena. By day 14 he developed melaena, dizziness and syncope, with blood pressure 90/47 mm Hg and pulse 128/min, requiring intensive care.
Haemoglobin was initially recorded as 92 g/L and later as 5.2 g/dL; the precise interval between these measurements is not supplied. Platelets were 368×10^9/L, INR 1.0 and aPTT 28 s.
Multiphasic CT showed duodenitis, possible contained ulcer perforation and blood in the stomach, but no active bleeding or pseudoaneurysm. Endoscopy found a posterior duodenal-bulb clot that could not be removed and a separate 5 mm clean-based ulcer. Subsequent angiography is not supplied.

case.opening: A man in his early 50s has 25 years of penetrating ileocolonic Crohn’s disease, previously controlled for three years with infliximab. Enterography 11 months earlier did not show a fistula.
case.initial_facts:
A man in his early 50s has 25 years of penetrating ileocolonic Crohn’s disease, previously controlled for three years with infliximab. Enterography 11 months earlier did not show a fistula.
He developed recurrent right testicular pain and swelling. Cultures over the course of repeated procedures grew different organisms, including Peptoniphilus, Bacteroides, Citrobacter, Proteus, E. coli, Klebsiella and Morganella. Epididymal/testicular surgery showed necrotising granulomatous inflammation. Acid-fast and fungal studies and selected PCR tests were negative. Brucella testing was not performed because no risk was identified; Bartonella testing was negative.
Later CT did not show active bowel disease or a fistula and he reported no gastrointestinal symptoms. Fresh cultures were not obtained at one later procedure; previous susceptibility results were used. Inflammation persisted despite prolonged antibiotics. Infliximab was held. Subsequent treatment and response are withheld.

One man has had three vascular presentations at different ages and sites.
In his 40s, tinnitus and temporal headache led to diagnosis of a left transverse/sigmoid dural arteriovenous fistula, type IIa+b with venous reflux. Three embolisations relieved symptoms and subsequent MRI remained clear for about 14 years.

In his 60s he developed right occipital pain, retromastoid tenderness and intermittent tinnitus. Angiography in 2018 showed a right transverse/sigmoid fistula classified as type I. case.title: New tumour findings after prolonged imatinib response

case.initial_facts:
A woman in her late 40s originally presented in 2001 with an approximately 8 cm gastric tumour and liver lesions. Initial metastatic-carcinoma treatment produced stable disease. Pathology review in 2002 showed KIT/CD34 positivity with negative desmin/cytokeratin and established GIST. KIT mutation testing was not performed then.
Imatinib began in 2002 at 400 mg daily, rose to 500 mg in 2004 and returned to 400 mg in 2016 because of renal/anaemia concerns. Renal function later declined to eGFR below 30 mL/min/1.73 m²; contrast CT was stopped from 2021.
After about 20.8 years of control, a distal-oesophageal prominence increased over two to three CT examinations across 1–2 years. In 2023 a 33 mm lesion was biopsied as GIST, with KIT, CD34 and DOG1 positivity. Sequencing found a KIT exon 11 driver and exon 13 V654A alteration associated with resistance. The original specimen was inadequate to verify its mutation. Later treatment and outcomes are not supplied.
