case.title: Fever, purpura and evolving renal findings
case.task_type: Reassessment of conflicting tests and multisystem evidence
case.decision_point: At the new admission, after imaging and initial repeated malaria smears, before skin biopsy and subsequent renal deterioration.
case.initial_facts:
A 65-year-old man with ulcerative colitis treated with mesalamine developed a prolonged illness after a sore throat. For about five weeks he has had fever, night sweats, arthralgia and abdominal symptoms. An earlier admission found inflammatory and liver-test abnormalities, but colonoscopy did not show active colitis. Antibiotics and a short prednisone course did not resolve the illness. A low-level EBV DNA result and positive viral-capsid IgM/IgG had led to a working diagnosis of primary EBV infection.
He later developed palpable purpura on the flanks and upper thighs, purpura on the lower legs, transient scrotal pain, joint pain and leg oedema. Earlier urinalyses were normal; at the new admission urine has 2+ protein, 1+ blood and 5–10 red cells/high-power field, with protein:creatinine ratio 0.99. Creatinine is 0.72 mg/dL, albumin 2.6 g/dL and platelets 505000/microlitre. CT shows small-bowel thickening, surrounding inflammatory change and small-volume ascites. He is febrile but haemodynamically stable and mentally alert.
He lived in West Africa and Southeast Asia more than ten years ago, travelled to Florida seven months ago and cleans a neighbour’s chicken coop. A rapid P. falciparum antigen test is positive, but thick and thin blood smears on two days are negative. Biopsy findings and later response are not supplied.

case.title: Persistent daytime sleep episodes despite improved mood
case.decision_point: At outpatient reassessment, before the planned antidepressant switch at this visit, objective sleep testing and subsequent sleep-specific treatment.
case.initial_facts:
A 24-year-old man has depression, anxiety and opioid-use disorder, with two previous unintentional overdoses. Treatment includes buprenorphine, venlafaxine and prazosin. Mood and anxiety improved during follow-up, but severe daytime sleepiness persisted despite reducing venlafaxine. He falls asleep unintentionally on public transport and while reading, and reports sometimes sleeping for very prolonged periods.
Further history includes brief hand weakness when laughing, visual/tactile experiences while falling asleep and repeated awakening with inability to move. His partner has not reported snoring or apnoea. Several relatives have unspecified sleep disorders. He reports no recent non-prescribed opioid use but has recently used ketamine several times a week and alcohol weekly. Routine testing detects buprenorphine and its metabolite but not other tested opioids, benzodiazepines or stimulants; it does not establish absence of every substance.
BMI is 21 and neurological examination is unremarkable. Selected renal, electrolyte, glucose, liver and iron studies are not explanatory. Thyroid testing is not supplied. There is no polysomnography or multiple-sleep-latency result at this point.
case.task: Audience: a clinician. Use 200–280 words in English. Distinguish fatigue from unintended sleep episodes, integrate the newly obtained sleep-related history and compare up to three explanations. Explain how psychiatric illness, medication and substance use can confound but need not settle the assessment. Propose the next evaluation and relevant safety discussion without declaring an unseen sleep-study result. Use only the supplied information at this decision point. Separate observed facts, hypotheses and proposed actions. Do not invent measurements, negative findings, treatment responses or probabilities. Do not give a drug dose or a fixed treatment regimen. Give concise clinical justifications, not a private reasoning trace.

case.reference: Provisional: the sleep episodes, emotion-related weakness, sleep paralysis and sleep-transition hallucinations support consideration of a central hypersomnolence disorder alongside medication, substance, psychiatric and other sleep causes. Refer for a sleep-focused assessment and appropriate objective testing; do not invent test results or normal thyroid studies. A limited toxicology panel does not exclude ketamine or every substance. The evidence justifies a working hypothesis, not importing the later MSLT conclusion. Safety advice and any medication changes require clinical review rather than copying the later regimen.

case.title: Progressive tremor, gait and cognitive symptoms after an initial head-injury label
case.task_type: Reassessment of an evolving neurological syndrome
case.decision_point: At readmission after continued deterioration, with initial EEG and CSF inflammation available but before pathogen-specific results and retrospective MRI clarification.
case.initial_facts:
A 59-year-old man in coastal southern Norway developed tremor, headache, night sweats and persistent hiccups after a fall with a blow to the back of the head. He has type 2 diabetes and previous thymoma surgery. An initial MRI was reported as unremarkable. Routine blood tests were not explanatory; the initial working diagnosis was post-concussion syndrome.
Symptoms progressed over months to gait difficulty, falls, memory difficulty, dysphagia, resting tremor, bradykinesia and hypophonia. Dopamine-transporter imaging showed reduced uptake, prompting a Parkinson disease hypothesis, but levodopa did not improve symptoms. He was readmitted with worsening weakness, wasting, brisk reflexes and possible fasciculations. Neurophysiological studies were normal. EEG showed mild encephalopathy, and CSF had 443 white cells/microlitre against a reference below 5, with protein 3.03 g/L.
There are no pathogen-specific CSF results, established cause, treatment response or formally reinterpreted MRI findings in this packet. A previously unremarkable report should not be rewritten as proof that no abnormality existed.

case.title: Recurrent destructive ulcers with systemic inflammatory features
case.decision_point: After several years of recurrent ulcers, biopsies and systemic workup, before the reported genetic investigation and later treatment success.
case.initial_facts:
A man first seen at age 41 has recurrent painful oropharyngeal ulceration causing dysphagia, followed by ulcers of the eyelids, tongue dorsum, lip mucosa and penis. Eyelid inflammation caused scarring and ocular surface complications; it is not described as uveitis. Over several years he also has periodic fever, lower-leg swelling/erythema, sicca symptoms, abdominal pain and diarrhoea.
Treatment and investigation have been complicated by infections, including severe C. difficile colitis after clindamycin for a suspected oropharyngeal infection, bowel perforation and resections. Multiple oral, skin and gastrointestinal specimens show non-specific changes without demonstrated granulomas or vasculitis; direct immunofluorescence is negative. No haematological malignancy was established by marrow, flow, protein, imaging and panel workup. Hilar lymphadenopathy was not found, and broad autoimmune serology was not explanatory.
No genetic result, final syndrome label or later response to immunomodulation is given. Negative or non-specific biopsies should be described precisely rather than turned into a universal exclusion rule.

case.title: Abrupt visual loss after intraocular lens exchange
case.task_type: Abrupt visual loss after intraocular lens exchange
case.decision_point: Thirty-minute postoperative assessment, before angiography, completed neuroimaging or visual recovery.
case.opening: A 40-year-old woman undergoes left intraocular lens exchange for recurrent vitreous haemorrhage attributed to uveitis–glaucoma–hyphaema syndrome. She previously had congenital cataract surgery with pars plana vitrectomy, lensectomy and posterior capsulotomy at age 13. Preoperative visual acuity was 20/30 in the left eye and 20/20 in the right. A sulcus single-piece lens has been replaced by a three-piece lens in a reportedly uncomplicated 15-minute procedure. Topical and intracameral agents included lidocaine and phenylephrine; the full medication record is available for review. About ten minutes later she reports complete left-eye visual loss. At thirty minutes she has no light perception and a marked relative afferent pupillary defect. Intraocular pressure is 8 mm Hg; the cornea is clear. Dilated examination describes an attached, perfused retina without visible detachment, choroidal haemorrhage, optic nerve pallor or vascular occlusion. She has mild ipsilateral supraorbital headache and no reported migraine or neurological history. Neuroimaging has been ordered, but no result is available.

Adaptation and hidden information

The source presentation and previous treatments are retained. The assessment stops before treatment starts. The question about evaluating evidence is study-authored; it is not a question posed in the paper. The later photographs, treatment response, monitoring and discussion conclusions are hidden during generation.

In the report, topical trametinib 0.02% was used twice daily. Symptoms improved within days, skin findings improved at six weeks and improvement persisted at six months. The authors call for larger series and controlled studies.

The childhood exposure is relevant to specialist assessment but does not alone establish the cause in this packet. Neurodegenerative, vascular/mixed and exposure-associated possibilities may be discussed. Pathology, genetic results and current imaging are not established in this packet.

case.title: Explaining a staged infant treatment plan
case.opening: Your infant son was diagnosed on day 24 through newborn screening and confirmatory testing with severe mucopolysaccharidosis type II. An IDS variant and undetectable relevant enzyme activity were found.
case.initial_facts:
Your infant son was diagnosed on day 24 through newborn screening and confirmatory testing with severe mucopolysaccharidosis type II. An IDS variant and undetectable relevant enzyme activity were found.
Intravenous enzyme replacement began at two months, and enzyme delivery into the brain’s fluid spaces began at three months. The specialist team is preparing a cord-blood transplant at nine months, after growth and donor coordination. The paper’s rationale is that blood-delivered treatment and transplant do not address brain involvement equally well in type II disease. Transplant outcomes, later development and complications are not yet available at this task’s decision point.
case.task: Audience: the infant’s parents. Use 220–280 words in plain English. Explain to the parents why the team is considering more than one treatment route, why treatment is staged, and what the plan cannot guarantee. Describe the broad risks and questions to discuss with the specialist team in accessible language. Do not give procedural instructions or promise a particular developmental outcome. Give brief evidence-based justifications, not a private reasoning trace. Do not invent unreported findings, ages, test results or outcomes. Do not prescribe a dose or claim that an unreported result is normal.

case.hidden: Infant 3 later had mild sinusoidal obstruction, a SARS-CoV-2 infection, no acute GVHD, and resumed brain-directed enzyme treatment on day 47. Follow-up outcomes, including developmental quotient, were not supplied. The prompt is a retrospective pretransplant adaptation, not a claim that all infants share these outcomes.
case.reference: Explain the missing-enzyme problem and the different access of systemic versus brain-directed treatment without implying identical effects in every mucopolysaccharidosis subtype. The stated growth/donor-coordination interval can be explained without inventing a universal optimal transplant age. Acknowledge transplant/procedure risks and uncertain long-term development; do not assume transplant outcomes or later development. case.title: Response denominators and a supportive-treatment claim
case.opening: A retrospective uncontrolled series treated 33 people with chemotherapy- or radiation-associated skin toxicity using high-dose oral vitamin D. Thirty also received concurrent supportive therapy.
case.initial_facts:
A retrospective uncontrolled series treated 33 people with chemotherapy- or radiation-associated skin toxicity using high-dose oral vitamin D. Thirty also received concurrent supportive therapy.
During the reported 10-day interval, 26 of 30 people with symptom data reported relief. Anticancer treatment continued without interruption in 24 of all 33. No treatment-related adverse events were reported. Post-treatment laboratory information was inconsistently available; post-treatment vitamin D levels were measured in 13. The packet supplies neither an untreated group nor patient-level pairing for every outcome.
case.task: Audience: a clinician. Use 180–240 words in English. Report the symptom-relief and uninterrupted-treatment percentages with their correct denominators. Explain what the results support about feasibility and observed improvement, and the limits of claims that vitamin D caused recovery or is generally safe. Do not substitute the full cohort denominator for a measured-outcome denominator. Give brief evidence-based justifications, not a private reasoning trace. Do not invent unreported findings, ages, test results or outcomes. Do not prescribe a dose or claim that an unreported result is normal.
case.decision_point: Assess only the information and task actually supplied at this point.
case.hidden: Other source analyses, erythema scores and mechanisms were not supplied and are not required. The source’s headline and abstract vary in how they describe 26 responders; this task prospectively uses the explicit Results denominator of 30.
case.reference: Symptom relief is 26/30, about 86.7%; uninterrupted therapy is 24/33, about 72.7%. The 30 measured people and 33 treated people are different denominators. Concurrent supportive treatments and natural recovery preclude attributing the observed outcome solely to vitamin D. No reported adverse events with incomplete follow-up is not proof of zero risk or universal safety. Do not equate no report with systematically verified absence in every patient.

case.title: Clinical shrinkage versus pathological response
case.opening: A prospective uncontrolled series enrolled 15 people with advanced cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma of the head and neck awaiting surgery. All received neoadjuvant capecitabine.
case.initial_facts:
A prospective uncontrolled series enrolled 15 people with advanced cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma of the head and neck awaiting surgery. All received neoadjuvant capecitabine.
Ten of 15 had clinical tumour reduction. Twelve underwent surgery; five of those twelve had a complete pathological response and seven of twelve were downstaged. Two people with apparent complete clinical lesion resolution chose radiotherapy instead of surgery; another did not proceed to surgery after progression. No grade 3 or higher treatment-related toxicity was reported. There was no comparator group, and follow-up for durability was short.
case.task: Audience: a clinician. Use 180–240 words in English. Give the clinical-reduction, pathological-complete-response and downstaging percentages with their denominators. Explain why clinical disappearance, pathological response and durable cure are different claims. State what can and cannot be concluded about comparative efficacy and safety. Give brief evidence-based justifications, not a private reasoning trace. Do not invent unreported findings, ages, test results or outcomes. Do not prescribe a dose or claim that an unreported result is normal.
case.decision_point: Assess only the information and task actually supplied at this point.
case.hidden: The source also gives dosing, individual tumour details and later interpretations, which are not supplied or required. No dose recommendation is requested. Recomputed percentages use one decimal place.
case.reference: Clinical reduction is 10/15 (66.7%); pathological complete response is 5/12 (41.7%) among surgically assessed people, not all 15; downstaging is 7/12 (58.3%). The two non-surgical clinical responders have no surgical pathology confirmation in this packet. No concurrent comparison or adequate long-term follow-up establishes superiority or durable cure. The absence of reported grade 3+ events is not absence of all toxicity or proof of safety for every subgroup.
